## 0. Description and Setup

### What this lab is about

This notebook complements the lecture *"Apache Spark - SQL API"*. It shows **different ways of using SQL within our Spark applications**. You'll learn how to:

| 🪟 1 · Create a temporary view | 🧾 2 · Query it with SQL | 🔁 3 · Get DataFrames back |
|---|---|---|
| Give a [DataFrame](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.DataFrame.html) a name that SQL can use: `createOrReplaceTempView()` | Manipulate the view with plain **SQL statements**: `spark_session.sql("SELECT …")` | Every SQL result **is a DataFrame**: keep transforming it, display it or save it |

We reuse part of the Spark analysis from lab 16.1, ***Transport for London, Bike point analysis***, so *you should already know most of the Spark code*. The new part is SQL.

### Two APIs, one engine

```
🐍 DataFrame API                          Spark SQL engine (Catalyst)                               result
bikepoint_df.where("key='NbBikes'")  ─┐   Unresolved logical plan → Analysis (names → 📚 catalog)
  .groupBy("id").agg(F.avg("value"))  ├─► → Optimisation (filters pushed, columns pruned)       ──►  DataFrame
🧾 SQL API                            │   → Physical plan (HashAggregate, Exchange…)
spark_session.sql("""SELECT id,      ─┘   → Execution: RDD tasks on the executors
  AVG(value) FROM BikePoints …""")        (the same job, whichever API you wrote)
```

Pick the API that reads best for each step; you can mix them in the same application.

### What we're going to build

```
STORAGE (from lab 16.1)            STEP 1 · DataFrame API                                STEP 2 · Temp views + SQL
MinIO bucket raw-data      s3a://  bikepoint_raw_df    read.json("…/bikepoints_*.json")  ─view─► BikePoints       ─sql─► min / max / avg bikes
bikepoints_…_2120.json      ──►    bikepoint_df        explode(additionalProperties)              BikePointsDocks  ─sql─► broken ratio per bike point
bikepoints_…_2125.json …           bikepoint_docks_df  … where key in (NbBikes, NbDocks, NbEmptyDocks)          → DataFrame → 🐼 .toPandas()
(NiFi drops one file every 5 min)
```

## Step 1. Create the Bike Point DataFrame for the Current Month

### Many files, one DataFrame: wildcards

You can create one DataFrame from many files ***by using wildcards (`*`) in the file names stored in MinIO***. More advanced patterns exist, but they're outside the scope of this course.

The file names follow the format **`bikepoints_yyyyMMdd_HHmm.json`**: `yyyy` year, `MM` month, `dd` day, `HH` hour (00–23), `mm` minute. Because the data is **partitioned by year, month, day and hour**, a wildcard picks the slice you need:

| Pattern | Files |
|---|---|
| `s3a://raw-data/bikepoints_*.json` | every file (what the notebook reads) |
| `s3a://raw-data/bikepoints_202611*_*.json` | the current month (November 2026; your dates will differ) |
| `s3a://raw-data/bikepoints_20261107_*.json` | one day |
| `s3a://raw-data/bikepoints_20261107_21*.json` | one hour |

> ⚠ The step title says "current month", but the notebook reads `bikepoints_*.json`. Change the pattern if your bucket holds older months.

You may also want to **add a column with the file name behind each row**. We don't use it in this lab, but it's handy for debugging and lineage.

### 1.1 DataFrame creation

We need to tell the SparkSession **how to access MinIO**, our *S3-compatible object store*:

```python
spark_session.sparkContext._jsc.hadoopConfiguration().set("fs.s3a.access.key", "s3access")
spark_session.sparkContext._jsc.hadoopConfiguration().set("fs.s3a.secret.key", "_s3access123$")
spark_session.sparkContext._jsc.hadoopConfiguration().set("fs.s3a.path.style.access", "true")
spark_session.sparkContext._jsc.hadoopConfiguration().set("fs.s3a.impl", "org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.S3AFileSystem")
spark_session.sparkContext._jsc.hadoopConfiguration().set("fs.s3a.endpoint", "http://localhost:9000")
```

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `access.key` / `secret.key` | MinIO user with access to the buckets |
| `path.style.access` | URLs like `host/bucket/key`, as MinIO expects |
| `impl` | the Hadoop S3A connector handles `s3a://` paths |
| `endpoint` | MinIO's **S3 API** (port 9000, not the console) |

**Cleaner alternative:** pass the same options when you build the session, with the `spark.hadoop.` prefix (`.config("spark.hadoop.fs.s3a.endpoint", "http://localhost:9000")` …). `_jsc` is an internal handle and isn't available on Spark Connect. Never commit real keys to Git: these are OSBDET's lab credentials.

We are now ready to **create the DataFrame from the data stored in MinIO**:

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import input_file_name

bikepoint_raw_df = spark_session.read\
                                .json("s3a://raw-data/bikepoints_*.json")

# DataFrame updated with an additional column containing the filename contributing to the data in every row.
bikepoint_raw_df = bikepoint_raw_df.withColumn("filename_path", input_file_name())

# The inferred schema can be visualized using the printSchema() method - definitely semi-structured data.
bikepoint_raw_df.printSchema()
```
```
root
 |-- $type: string (nullable = true)
 |-- additionalProperties: array (nullable = true)
 |    |-- element: struct (containsNull = true)
 |    |    |-- $type: string (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- category: string (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- key: string (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- modified: string (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- sourceSystemKey: string (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- value: string (nullable = true)
 |-- children: array (nullable = true)
 |    |-- element: string (containsNull = true)
 |-- childrenUrls: array (nullable = true)
 |    |-- element: string (containsNull = true)
 |-- commonName: string (nullable = true)
 |-- id: string (nullable = true)
 |-- lat: double (nullable = true)
 |-- lon: double (nullable = true)
 |-- placeType: string (nullable = true)
 |-- url: string (nullable = true)
 |-- filename_path: string (nullable = false)
```

**Modern alternative:** `F.col("_metadata.file_path")` (Spark ≥ 3.3) gives the same information. `input_file_name()` is deprecated on Databricks and isn't supported with Unity Catalog.

### 1.2 Shaping the DataFrame to answer business questions

Once your files are in the batch storage layer, your goals are:

1. ***Define the logic you need*** to implement in Spark to answer the business questions.
2. ***Adapt the initial "raw" DataFrame*** into a structure that makes that logic simple. This approach is called ["Schema on Read"](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/what-is-schema-on-read-and-schema-on-write-in-hadoop/), and it's a very powerful way to make the most of the data in your storage layer.
3. ***Translate the logic into Spark code***: today, much of it in SQL.

The business question is ***"What are the minimum, maximum and average numbers of bikes used during the current month?"***, so we need a DataFrame with:

1. ***The identifier of each bike point*** and its name
2. ***The GPS location of each bike point***, in case we want to plot the results on a map later
3. ***The number of bikes*** per bike point over time

> ⚠ **Precision:** `NbBikes` counts bikes **docked and available** at the station, not bikes in use (see lab 16.1). We keep the notebook's wording but read it that way.

```python
from pyspark.sql.functions import explode

bikepoint_df = bikepoint_raw_df.withColumn("additional", explode("additionalProperties"))\
                               .select("id", "commonName", "lat", "lon",
                                       "additional.key","additional.value","additional.modified")
bikepoint_df.printSchema()
```
```
root
 |-- id: string (nullable = true)
 |-- commonName: string (nullable = true)
 |-- lat: double (nullable = true)
 |-- lon: double (nullable = true)
 |-- key: string (nullable = true)
 |-- value: string (nullable = true)
 |-- modified: string (nullable = true)
```

```
1 row: BikePoints_1 · River Street · [{TerminalName}, {Installed}, … ×11]
        ──explode──►  11 rows: BikePoints_1 · … · {TerminalName}
                               BikePoints_1 · … · {Installed}
                               …
                               BikePoints_1 · … · {NbBikes: 4}
                               …
3,188 rows × 11 = 35,068 rows
```

The result is a flat, **long** table: one row per (bike point, property, snapshot). `value` is a **string** for every property. Remember that.

```python
bikepoint_df.limit(10).toPandas()
```

## Step 2. Temporary View Creation

### Managing temporary views: three functions

We *simplify temporary view management* to the following **three functions** (the notebook says "two" and lists three):

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| **[`DataFrame.createOrReplaceTempView()`](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.DataFrame.createOrReplaceTempView.html)** | **Creates or replaces a local temporary view** with the referenced DataFrame. Its lifetime is tied to the **SparkSession** that was used to create the DataFrame. |
| **[`pyspark.sql.Catalog.dropTempView()`](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.Catalog.dropTempView.html)** | **Drops the local temporary view** with the given name from the catalog. The Catalog is accessible through the **[`catalog`](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.SparkSession.catalog.html) property** of the SparkSession *we always create at the beginning of our Spark applications*. |
| **[`pyspark.sql.Catalog.listTables()`](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.Catalog.listTables.html)** | Returns the list of tables and views in the current SparkSession. |

```
SparkSession · catalog:   BikePoints ──points to──► bikepoint_df (a plan, not a copy) ┄┄reads when queried┄┄► MinIO raw-data
The view lives as long as the session. Stop the session → the view is gone; the files stay.
```

| Variant | Difference |
|---|---|
| `createTempView` | fails if the name already exists (`TEMP_TABLE_OR_VIEW_ALREADY_EXISTS`) |
| `createOrReplaceGlobalTempView` | shared by all sessions of the application, queried as `global_temp.name` |

Let's display the *number of available views* before doing anything:

```python
spark_session.catalog.listTables()
```
```
[]
```

Let's **create a new view** called `BikePoints` from the `bikepoint_df` DataFrame:

```python
bikepoint_df.createOrReplaceTempView("BikePoints")
```

And display the *number of available views* after the previous statement:

```python
spark_session.catalog.listTables()
```
```
[Table(name='BikePoints', catalog=None, namespace=[], description=None, tableType='TEMPORARY', isTemporary=True)]
```

- `createOrReplaceTempView` returns nothing and **runs no job**: it only registers a name in the catalog.
- `tableType='TEMPORARY'`, `isTemporary=True`: the view belongs to this session. `catalog=None` because temp views live outside any database. Spark 4 lists it in lower case (`'bikepoints'`), because names are case-insensitive.
- Run the cell twice and nothing breaks: the view is simply **replaced**.

> ✓ **Checkpoint:** `listTables()` shows `BikePoints`. From now on, SQL can use that name.

### 2.1 Temporary view SQL manipulation

Temporary views are manipulated with one **function**:

* **[`SparkSession.sql()`](https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/api/python/reference/pyspark.sql/api/pyspark.sql.SparkSession.sql.html)**: returns a DataFrame with the result of the given query.

Let's answer the business question, ***"what are the minimum, maximum and average bikes used in the current month?"***, with SQL:

```python
spark_session.sql("""SELECT id, key, MIN(value), MAX(value), AVG(value)
                     FROM BikePoints
                     WHERE key='NbBikes'
                     GROUP BY id,key""")\
             .limit(10)\
             .toPandas()
```

| | id | key | min(value) | max(value) | avg(value) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | BikePoints_1 | NbBikes | 4 | 4 | 4.00 |
| 1 | BikePoints_10 | NbBikes | 12 | 12 | 12.00 |
| 2 | BikePoints_101 | NbBikes | 4 | 5 | 4.25 |
| 3 | BikePoints_102 | NbBikes | 1 | 3 | 2.00 |
| 4 | BikePoints_103 | NbBikes | 1 | 2 | 1.75 |
| 5 | BikePoints_104 | NbBikes | 10 | 11 | 10.25 |
| 6 | BikePoints_105 | NbBikes | 3 | 3 | 3.00 |
| 7 | BikePoints_106 | NbBikes | 1 | 1 | 1.00 |
| 8 | BikePoints_107 | NbBikes | 5 | 5 | 5.00 |
| 9 | BikePoints_109 | NbBikes | 44 | 45 | 44.25 |

The result has 797 rows, one per bike point with 4 snapshots each: exactly the same numbers as lab 16.1's DataFrame version.

#### ⚠ Same trap, now in SQL: MIN and MAX of text

`value` is a **string**, so `MIN` and `MAX` compare **alphabetically** (`"13" < "9"`). `AVG` is fine because Spark casts the text to numbers to add it up.

```sql
-- how many bike points get a wrong min or max?
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
  SELECT id, MIN(value) AS mn, MAX(value) AS mx,
         MIN(CAST(value AS INT)) AS rmn, MAX(CAST(value AS INT)) AS rmx
  FROM BikePoints WHERE key = 'NbBikes' GROUP BY id)
WHERE mn <> CAST(rmn AS STRING) OR mx <> CAST(rmx AS STRING)
```
```
[Row(count(1)=17)]      # 17 of 797 bike points
```

An improved answer, still 100% SQL:

```python
spark_session.sql("""
  SELECT id, commonName,
         MIN(CAST(value AS INT))           AS min_bikes,
         MAX(CAST(value AS INT))           AS max_bikes,
         ROUND(AVG(CAST(value AS INT)), 2) AS avg_bikes,
         COUNT(*)                          AS samples
  FROM BikePoints
  WHERE key = 'NbBikes'
  GROUP BY id, commonName
  ORDER BY id""").limit(5).toPandas()
```

| | id | commonName | min_bikes | max_bikes | avg_bikes | samples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | BikePoints_1 | River Street , Clerkenwell | 4 | 4 | 4.00 | 4 |
| 1 | BikePoints_10 | Park Street, Bankside | 12 | 12 | 12.00 | 4 |
| 2 | BikePoints_101 | Queen Street 1, Bank | 4 | 5 | 4.25 | 4 |
| 3 | BikePoints_102 | Jewry Street, Aldgate | 1 | 3 | 2.00 | 4 |
| 4 | BikePoints_103 | Vicarage Gate, Kensington | 1 | 2 | 1.75 | 4 |

The improved query returns numbers, readable names, **aliases** (no more `min(value)` column names) and a sample count; `ORDER BY` makes the output repeatable.

### 2.2 DataFrame from results after temporary view manipulation

**Nothing special** is needed to turn the result of `SparkSession.sql()` into a DataFrame, because the function already returns one:

```python
spark_session.sql("""SELECT id, key, MIN(value), MAX(value), AVG(value)
                     FROM BikePoints
                     WHERE key='NbBikes'
                     GROUP BY id,key""")
```
```
DataFrame[id: string, key: string, min(value): string, max(value): string, avg(value): double]
```

```python
spark_session.sql("""SELECT id, key, MIN(value), MAX(value), AVG(value)
                     FROM BikePoints
                     WHERE key='NbBikes'
                     GROUP BY id,key""")\
              .printSchema()
```
```
root
 |-- id: string (nullable = true)
 |-- key: string (nullable = true)
 |-- min(value): string (nullable = true)
 |-- max(value): string (nullable = true)
 |-- avg(value): double (nullable = true)
```

- The first cell prints **only the schema**: `sql()` is **lazy**, like any transformation. No job runs until an action (`toPandas`, `count`, `show`…).
- The schema confirms the trap: `min` and `max` are **strings**; only `avg` is a double.
- Column names like `min(value)` are awkward in later code, so **alias them** in SQL (`AS min_bikes`).

**Mix both APIs freely:**

```python
stats_df = spark_session.sql("""SELECT id, commonName,
       ROUND(AVG(CAST(value AS INT)), 2) AS avg_bikes
  FROM BikePoints WHERE key = 'NbBikes'
  GROUP BY id, commonName""")

stats_df.where("avg_bikes >= 30").orderBy(F.desc("avg_bikes")).limit(5).toPandas()   # DataFrame API on a SQL result

stats_df.createOrReplaceTempView("BikePointStats")                                   # …and back to SQL
```

| | id | commonName | avg_bikes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | BikePoints_109 | Soho Square , Soho | 44.25 |
| 1 | BikePoints_194 | Hop Exchange, The Borough | 41.00 |
| 2 | BikePoints_532 | Jubilee Plaza, Canary Wharf | 35.25 |
| 3 | BikePoints_362 | Royal College Street, Camden Town | 35.00 |
| 4 | BikePoints_409 | Strata, Elephant & Castle | 34.25 |

#### Proof: SQL and the DataFrame API run the same plan

```python
spark_session.sql("""SELECT id, AVG(CAST(value AS INT)) AS avg_bikes
  FROM BikePoints WHERE key = 'NbBikes' GROUP BY id""").explain()

bikepoint_df.where("key = 'NbBikes'").groupBy("id")\
  .agg(F.avg(F.col("value").cast("int")).alias("avg_bikes")).explain()
```
```
== Physical Plan ==                    # identical for both (expression ids removed)
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=false
+- HashAggregate(keys=[id], functions=[avg(cast(value as int))])
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(id, 200)
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[id], functions=[partial_avg(cast(value as int))])
         +- Project [id, additional.value AS value]
            +- Filter (isnotnull(additional.key) AND (additional.key = NbBikes))
               +- Generate explode(additionalProperties)
                  +- Filter ((size(additionalProperties) > 0) AND isnotnull(additionalProperties))
                     +- FileScan json [additionalProperties, id] PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(additionalProperties)]
```

![Spark UI, SQL / DataFrame tab: the view creation, the SQL query and the DataFrame API query](data:image/webp;base64,)

- Catalyst **reads only the two columns it needs** (`additionalProperties`, `id`) and filters before the shuffle (`Exchange`).
- There's no performance difference between the two APIs, so choose the one that **reads best** for each step. (The second run in the Spark UI is faster only because of warm-up: JVM and file caches.)

#### Cheat sheet: SQL ⇄ DataFrame API

| SQL (`spark_session.sql`) | DataFrame API (`import pyspark.sql.functions as F`) |
|---|---|
| `SELECT id, commonName AS name` | `df.select("id", F.col("commonName").alias("name"))` |
| `WHERE key = 'NbBikes'` | `df.where("key = 'NbBikes'")` · `df.filter(F.col("key") == "NbBikes")` |
| `GROUP BY id` + `MIN / MAX / AVG / COUNT` | `df.groupBy("id").agg(F.min(…), F.max(…), F.avg(…), F.count("*"))` |
| `CAST(value AS INT)` | `F.col("value").cast("int")` |
| `CASE WHEN … THEN … ELSE … END` | `F.when(…, …).otherwise(…)` |
| `HAVING avg_bikes > 10` | `.where("avg_bikes > 10")` after the `agg` |
| `ORDER BY avg_bikes DESC LIMIT 5` | `.orderBy(F.desc("avg_bikes")).limit(5)` |
| `a JOIN b USING (id)` | `a.join(b, "id")` |
| `WITH t AS (…) SELECT … FROM t` | a Python variable holding an intermediate DataFrame |
| `LATERAL VIEW explode(additionalProperties) t AS additional` | `.withColumn("additional", F.explode("additionalProperties"))` |

### 2.3 SQL challenge with Spark SQL

Let's answer a more elaborate business question with SQL: ***"Display BikePoints with a broken-bike ratio greater than 0% in the currently ingested data"***, where ***# of broken bikes = NbDocks − NbBikes − NbEmptyDocks***.

```
River Street, Clerkenwell · 19 docks:  [ 4 bikes ][ 8 empty ][ 7 "broken" ]
19 − 4 − 8 = 7 docks that are neither available bikes nor free → ratio = 7 / 19 = 36.8% (first snapshot)
```

Our Data Engineering team has created the following DataFrame containing the information for `NbBikes`, `NbDocks` and `NbEmptyDocks`:

```python
from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType
import pyspark.sql.functions as F

bikepoint_docks_df = \
```

#### Your turn: the two TBD cells

1. **[TBD] Create a new view.** *The previously created view is not the right one for this question*, so register `bikepoint_docks_df` under a new name, e.g. `BikePointsDocks`.
2. **[TBD] Answer with SQL.** Return one row per bike point with its docks, bikes, empty docks, broken count and **broken ratio**, keeping only ratios > 0%.

**Hints:**
- The data is **long** (one row per property) and you need it **wide** (one column per property). Use **conditional aggregation**: `SUM(CASE WHEN key = 'NbDocks' THEN CAST(value AS INT) END)`.
- `value` is text, so **cast** it.
- Compute the totals in a **CTE** (`WITH totals AS (…)`), then compute the ratio over it.
- Multiply by `100.0`, not `100`, to keep decimals.
- Filter `WHERE broken > 0` and `ORDER BY` the ratio.

```
id    key           value                     id    bikes  empty  docks
BP_1  NbBikes       4        ──pivot──►        BP_1  4      8      19
BP_1  NbEmptyDocks  8
BP_1  NbDocks       19
```

> **Try it before reading the solution.** 15 minutes, in pairs.

<details>
<summary><strong>Solution</strong></summary>

```python
# [TBD 1] Since the previously created view is no longer valid for this question, create a new one
bikepoint_docks_df.createOrReplaceTempView("BikePointsDocks")

# [TBD 2] Answer the business question with SQL
broken_df = spark_session.sql("""
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT id, commonName,
    SUM(CASE WHEN key = 'NbDocks'      THEN CAST(value AS INT) END) AS docks,
    SUM(CASE WHEN key = 'NbBikes'      THEN CAST(value AS INT) END) AS bikes,
    SUM(CASE WHEN key = 'NbEmptyDocks' THEN CAST(value AS INT) END) AS empty_docks
  FROM BikePointsDocks
  GROUP BY id, commonName)
SELECT id, commonName, docks, bikes, empty_docks,
       docks - bikes - empty_docks AS broken,
       ROUND((docks - bikes - empty_docks) * 100.0 / docks, 2) AS broken_ratio_pct
FROM totals
WHERE docks - bikes - empty_docks > 0
ORDER BY broken_ratio_pct DESC, id""")

broken_df.limit(10).toPandas()
```

```python
broken_df.count()
```

```
643        # of 797 bike points
```

- These are sums over the 4 snapshots (River Street has 19 docks × 4 = 76). The **ratio** is still right, because every term is summed over the same snapshots.
- `CASE` without `ELSE` gives `NULL`, which `SUM` ignores.

</details>

#### Reading the answer critically

| All London, same 4 snapshots | Dock-snapshots | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Available bikes | 34,459 | 41.1% |
| Empty docks | 43,450 | 51.8% |
| "Broken" (neither) | 5,943 | **7.09%** |
| **Total docks** | **83,852** | 100% |

**643 of 797** stations (81%) have at least one.

> ⚠ **What does the gap really measure?** [TfL's tech forum](https://techforum.tfl.gov.uk/t/bikepoint-api-clarifications/2732) explains that a dock that is **out of service** is not counted in `NbBikes` or `NbEmptyDocks`. So the gap counts **unavailable docks**: a broken bike locked in a dock is one possible cause and a faulty dock is another, and the data can't tell them apart. "Broken-bike ratio" is the notebook's simplification, so say so in your report.

- **Another trap:** `modified` is *not* a snapshot id. When a station hasn't changed, its `modified` is the same in several files (562 stations had one value across all 4). To compare snapshots, group by `filename_path` instead.
- Ranking by ratio favours small stations. Adding `AND docks >= 80` (20 docks × 4 snapshots) is a sensible extra filter.

#### Two other ways to go from long to wide

**SQL · PIVOT clause (Spark ≥ 2.4):**

```python
spark_session.sql("""
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT id, commonName, key, CAST(value AS INT) AS v FROM BikePointsDocks)
PIVOT (SUM(v) FOR key IN ('NbDocks' AS docks, 'NbBikes' AS bikes, 'NbEmptyDocks' AS empty_docks))
ORDER BY id""").limit(5).toPandas()
```

| | id | commonName | docks | bikes | empty_docks |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | BikePoints_1 | River Street , Clerkenwell | 76 | 16 | 32 |
| 1 | BikePoints_10 | Park Street, Bankside | 72 | 48 | 20 |
| 2 | BikePoints_101 | Queen Street 1, Bank | 88 | 17 | 59 |
| 3 | BikePoints_102 | Jewry Street, Aldgate | 68 | 8 | 48 |
| 4 | BikePoints_103 | Vicarage Gate, Kensington | 72 | 7 | 61 |

**DataFrame API · `groupBy().pivot()`:**

```python
wide_df = bikepoint_docks_df.withColumn("v", F.col("value").cast("int"))\
  .groupBy("id", "commonName")\
  .pivot("key", ["NbDocks", "NbBikes", "NbEmptyDocks"])\
  .sum("v")

broken_df2 = wide_df\
  .withColumn("broken", F.expr("NbDocks - NbBikes - NbEmptyDocks"))\
  .withColumn("broken_ratio_pct", F.round(F.col("broken") * 100 / F.col("NbDocks"), 2))\
  .where("broken > 0")

broken_df2.count()        # 643, as in SQL
```

Listing the pivot values saves Spark an extra job to find them. That makes three ways, one plan family and one answer, so use the one your team reads best.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Path does not exist: s3a://raw-data/bikepoints_*.json` | No files in `raw-data` | Run lab 16.1's NiFi flow for 10–15 minutes |
| Connection refused on `localhost:9000` · `403` | MinIO off · wrong keys | Turn MinIO on · re-run the `fs.s3a.*` cell |
| `[TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND] … BikePoints` | View not created yet, created in another session, or session restarted | Re-run `createOrReplaceTempView` after every kernel restart |
| `[TEMP_TABLE_OR_VIEW_ALREADY_EXISTS]` | `createTempView` run twice | Use `createOrReplaceTempView` |
| `[PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR]` | Typo, missing comma, or Python quotes clashing with SQL quotes | Triple quotes outside, single quotes for SQL strings |
| `[UNRESOLVED_COLUMN]` on `min(value)` | Unaliased aggregate names | Alias in SQL (`AS min_bikes`) or use backticks |
| max smaller than min | `value` is a string | `CAST(value AS INT)` before aggregating |
| Ratio is always 0 | Integer division | Multiply by `100.0`, not `100` |
